newsitem.title: UK: Study finds area of brain linked with depression.
newsitem.headline: Study finds area of brain linked with depression.

text.p: U.S. researchers said on Wednesday they had found more evidence of a physical cause of depression by identifying an area of the brain that is under-active in some depressed people.

Wayne Revets and colleagues at the Washington University School of Medicine in St Louis said the prefrontal cortex -- the area detached during a frontal lobotomy operation -- was exceptionally inactive.

Writing in the science journal Nature, they said they used positron emission tomography (PET) scans to show that the prefrontal cortex was consistently quiet in depressed patients with a family history of depression and in manic-depressives.

The same region became activated during manic episodes. This could be because the synapses -- the connections between brain cells -- were firing less often, or because the area had atrophied due to lower blood flow.
Using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), they found the size of the profrontal cortex was reduced in the left side of the brain in depressed patients but not in healthy volunteers.

"They have identified a key player in one of the several systems that underlie emotional processing -- a valuable finding indeed," Antonio Damasio, a neurologist at the University of Iowa, wrote in a commentary.

"The overall region identified in their study has been implicated in the modulation of neurotransmitters such as serotonin, noradrenaline and dopamine, whose levels are manipulated by anti-depressant drugs."
The findings, added to other research, indicated that the prefrontal cortex was critical to emotions related to personal and social situations, said Damasio, a prominent researcher in the field.

Prefrontal lobotomies were once performed to calm agitated mental patients. Featured in the film "One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest," the procedure can calm people with mental disorders but also damages initiative and spontaneity.
